title: Sorting and Limiting
summary: Sort by any column in either direction, break ties, take the top rows, and remove duplicates.
intro: A table has no order of its own, and real questions often need one: the highest paid, the newest hires, the first page of results. This lesson sorts rows with `ORDER BY`, cuts them down with `LIMIT` and `OFFSET`, and removes repeats with `DISTINCT`.
setup:
CREATE TABLE employees (
    id integer PRIMARY KEY,
    name text,
    department text,
    title text,
    salary integer,
    hired date
);

steps.title: Sorting both ways
steps.body:
Every program in this lesson uses an `employees` table with 10 rows. Here are the columns and the first few rows:

```sql harness
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS employees CASCADE;
{{code}}
```

```sql
CREATE TABLE employees (id integer PRIMARY KEY, name text, department text,
    title text, salary integer, hired date);
```

```text
 id | name  | department  |      title      | salary |   hired
----+-------+-------------+-----------------+--------+------------
  1 | Ana   | Engineering | Developer       |  95000 | 2021-03-15
  2 | Ben   | Sales       | Account Manager |  62000 | 2019-07-01
  3 | Chloe | Engineering | Developer       |  88000 | 2022-01-10
  4 | Dev   | Marketing   | Designer        |  58000 | 2020-11-23
```

`ORDER BY` sorts the result. Each column sorts ascending (`ASC`, the default) unless you write `DESC` right after it. `DESC` applies only to the column it follows:

```sql
SELECT name, department, salary FROM employees
ORDER BY salary DESC;          -- highest first
SELECT name, department, salary FROM employees
ORDER BY department, salary DESC;
```

With several columns, PostgreSQL sorts by the first, and only rows that tie on it are sorted by the second, and so on. Numbers sort from smallest to largest and dates from earliest to latest. Text sorts by character code in this database, which is A to Z when the case matches, but every capital letter comes before every lowercase one, so `Zoe` sorts before `adam`.

Two rows can still tie on every column you listed. Their order is then not guaranteed and can change between runs. So end the list with a unique column such as `id` to break any tie that is left.

example.prompt: List everyone grouped by department, highest salary first inside each department.

practice.title: Newest hires first
practice.prompt:
List every employee by hire date, newest first, with fixed tie breakers.

1. Select `name` and `hired` from `employees`.
2. Sort by `hired`, latest date first.
3. When two people were hired on the same day, sort them by `name` A to Z.
4. End the sort with `id` so even two people with the same name and date keep a fixed order.

Expected output:

```text
 name  |   hired
-------+------------
 Hugo  | 2024-04-01
 Ema   | 2023-02-06
 Jon   | 2022-08-15
 Chloe | 2022-01-10
 Ana   | 2021-03-15
 Dev   | 2020-11-23
 Iris  | 2020-06-08
 Gina  | 2019-09-30
 Ben   | 2019-07-01
 Farid | 2018-05-14
(10 rows)
```

steps.title: Top rows and pages
steps.body:
`LIMIT n` keeps only the first `n` rows of the sorted result. `OFFSET n` skips `n` rows first, which is how you get the next page. The last page can be short, or empty when `OFFSET` skips past every row:

```sql
SELECT id, name FROM employees ORDER BY id
LIMIT 3;            -- rows 1 to 3
SELECT id, name FROM employees ORDER BY id
LIMIT 3 OFFSET 3;   -- rows 4 to 6
SELECT id, name FROM employees ORDER BY id
LIMIT 3 OFFSET 6;   -- rows 7 to 9
```

`LIMIT` without `ORDER BY` returns some rows, not the top rows, so always sort first. And sort on columns that never tie: if two rows tie at the edge of a page, one could show up on both pages or on neither.

`ORDER BY` runs after the `SELECT` list, so it can use a column alias:

```sql
SELECT name, salary + 2000 AS with_raise
FROM employees
ORDER BY with_raise DESC, id;
```

Use the alias on its own. `WHERE` cannot see it, and neither can an expression like `ORDER BY with_raise + 1`.

example.title: Pay pages
example.prompt: Show the 3 highest paid employees with a 2000 raise added, then the next page of 3.
example.code:
-- The 3 highest paid
SELECT name, salary, salary + 2000 AS with_raise
FROM employees
ORDER BY with_raise DESC, id
LIMIT 3;

-- The next page: rows 4 to 6
SELECT name, salary, salary + 2000 AS with_raise
FROM employees
ORDER BY with_raise DESC, id
LIMIT 3 OFFSET 3;
example.explanation: Both queries sort the same way, by the `with_raise` alias from highest to lowest, with `id` as the tie breaker. The first keeps rows 1 to 3. The second skips those 3 with `OFFSET 3` and keeps the next 3. Chloe and Iris tie at 90000, and `id` puts Chloe on page one and Iris on page two every time.

practice.title: Earliest hires
practice.prompt:
Show the 2 earliest hires, then the next 2.

1. In both queries, select `name` and `hired` as `start_date` from `employees`.
2. Sort by the `start_date` alias, earliest first, then by `id`.
3. The first query keeps 2 rows.
4. The second query skips 2 rows and keeps the next 2.

Expected output:

```text
 name  | start_date
-------+------------
 Farid | 2018-05-14
 Ben   | 2019-07-01
(2 rows)

 name | start_date
------+------------
 Gina | 2019-09-30
 Iris | 2020-06-08
(2 rows)
```
practice.starter:
-- The 2 earliest hires
SELECT name, hired AS start_date
FROM employees
ORDER BY id; -- TODO: sort by start_date and keep 2 rows

-- The next 2
SELECT name, hired AS start_date
FROM employees
ORDER BY id; -- TODO: sort the same way, skip 2 rows, keep 2
practice.solution:
-- The 2 earliest hires
SELECT name, hired AS start_date
FROM employees
ORDER BY start_date, id
LIMIT 2;

-- The next 2
SELECT name, hired AS start_date
FROM employees
ORDER BY start_date, id
LIMIT 2 OFFSET 2;
hints: Dates sort earliest first by default, so no `DESC` is needed.
Both queries sort the same way. The second one also skips the first page with `OFFSET`.

steps.title: Removing duplicates
steps.body:
`SELECT DISTINCT` keeps one copy of each different row in the result:

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT department
FROM employees
ORDER BY department;
```

With several columns, `DISTINCT` compares the whole row, not just the first column. `SELECT DISTINCT department, title` keeps each different pair once, so a department still shows up once for every title it has. Parentheses do not change that: `SELECT DISTINCT (department), title` still compares both columns.

Since every row left is different, sorting by all the selected columns never ties. One rule to know: with `DISTINCT`, every `ORDER BY` column must be in the `SELECT` list. Sorting distinct departments by `id` fails, because each department has many ids:

```sql error
SELECT DISTINCT department
FROM employees
ORDER BY id;
```

```text
ERROR:  for SELECT DISTINCT, ORDER BY expressions must appear in select list
```

Try it in the editor to see the error.

recap:
- `ORDER BY a, b DESC` sorts by `a` ascending, then ties by `b` descending. `DESC` applies to one column.
- End the sort with a unique column like `id` so ties always come out the same way.
- `LIMIT n` keeps the first `n` rows and `OFFSET n` skips `n` rows. Always sort before you limit.
- `ORDER BY` can use a `SELECT` alias on its own.
- `SELECT DISTINCT` removes repeated rows, comparing every selected column.
- With `DISTINCT`, every `ORDER BY` column must be in the `SELECT` list.
